A1.justification: Despite the new title and substantial refocusing, both PDFs describe the same work, retaining adversarial learning on advantage functions, monotonicity arguments, and expert-policy aggregation. Both are readable throughout, including v1 Appendices A–F and v2 Appendices A–B.

before.justification: V1 Section 6 and Appendix E report original stochastic matching simulations, including numerical policy values, learning curves, expert-composition analyses, and uncertainty across repeated runs.

after.justification: V2 contains theoretical results and an algorithm illustration, but no original empirical outcomes. Its abstract and Section 8 explicitly leave empirical evaluation to future research; the appendices contain proofs.

M1.justification: The advantage-based learning principle remains, but v2 adapts updates to stage-specific policies in episodic adversarial MDPs and offers Q-value-based alternatives for general learners. V1's concrete truncated-rollout estimator, Bernoulli state sampling, and lazy-update variant disappear; v2 Section 8 instead proposes updates using generic bounded value estimates.

E1.justification: V1's entire empirical coverage is removed: stochastic matching scenarios with four and eight item classes and different compatibility graphs (Section 6 and Appendix E). V2 introduces no evaluated replacement tasks; its broader adversarial-MDP setting is theoretical.

E2.justification: V2 removes all evaluated comparisons. V1 compares polynomial, fixed-rate exponential, and varying-rate exponential updates, plus greedy projection in Scenario 1, alongside individual matching experts and optimal-policy benchmarks. Methods discussed or illustrated in v2 are not empirically evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The simulation protocols disappear, including exact Bellman-value evaluation from initially empty queues, the 2,500-step and 2,000,000-step learning runs, and sampled-state versus visited-state updates in Appendix E. V2 supplies no replacement experimental protocol.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix E's supplementary analysis of optimal-mixture composition is removed. For example, Scenario 1 assigns fractions 0.48, 0.50, and 0.02 of states to the three experts, examining whether individually weaker experts still contribute. V2 has no corresponding analysis; this is a limited loss beyond the removed benchmark scores.

E5.justification: V1 reports averages over 20 repetitions in Scenario 1 and five in Scenario 2, with shaded bands representing plus or minus two standard errors. V2 removes this empirical repeated-run and uncertainty reporting entirely.

E6.justification: All simulation values and learning curves are removed. For example, v1 reports optimal-mixture versus best-single-expert values of 138.18 versus 136.80 in Scenario 1 and 364.00 versus 363.92 in Scenario 2. V2 reports no replacement empirical results, so no cross-version performance improvement can be inferred.

T1.justification: V2 reworks the discounted, fixed-reward theory for episodic adversarial rewards and adds strongly adaptive regret, tracking regret, and a regime-dependent exponential-weights bound (Sections 5–6 and Appendix A). Existing monotonicity and last-iterate arguments are adapted, not newly introduced. V1's explicit estimator-specific expectation and high-probability theorems are removed; v2 adds an episodic performance-difference proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction shift from expert-orchestration modeling, explicit estimated-advantage guarantees, and simulations to a general adversarial-MDP reduction, stronger regret criteria, and interchangeable policy-improvement strategies. Practical performance becomes a future-research proposition rather than an illustrated contribution.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive applicability qualifications: evolving experts would invalidate the fixed-transition reduction, and estimation errors can dominate improved oracle bounds. Sections 3.3 and 8 discuss potential stability and variance benefits of advantage-based updates while leaving their empirical impact unresolved. V1's estimator-specific limitations and matching-result interpretations disappear.

D1.justification: V1's graph, reward, arrival-generation, hyperparameter, learning-rate, and rollout implementation details in Appendices B–E are removed. V2 instead supplies a generic estimated-value interface, an algorithm-modification schematic, and a pointer to the third-party Opera package for future studies, without a replacement simulation recipe.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly credits Shani et al. (2020) for the underlying reduction and substantially expands positioning around adversarial MDPs, adaptive regret, and learning from multiple oracles. Its discussions of Cheng et al. (2020), Liu et al. (2023), and other policy-optimization work replace v1's emphasis on ensemble orchestration and a 'third way' between value learning and policy gradients.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and extensively rewritten and reorganized. Direct tabular optimization becomes the starting point, expert aggregation moves to Section 7, existing monotonicity material enters the main text, and future empirical directions replace the simulation ending. Six supplementary sections are replaced by two proof appendices.

P2.justification: V1's two-column main text becomes a single-column article. Matching graphs, numerical tables, and learning-curve plots disappear. V2 redesigns the setting boxes, adds a side-by-side tabular-versus-aggregation summary, and introduces Figure 1 illustrating modifications to Shani et al.'s policy-improvement step.

improvement.justification: V2 provides broader theoretical coverage, clearer attribution of the underlying reduction, and proofs for adaptive, tracking, and regime-dependent guarantees. However, it removes v1's self-contained estimation procedure and associated guarantees, together with both simulation studies; Section 8 offers general guidance and untested practical expectations instead. These substantial theoretical gains coexist with losses in practical completeness and supporting evidence. The PDFs do not establish a reliable net direction in overall quality.
